wars.name: Conquest of Transalpine Gaul (Saluvian and Allobrogian wars)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; creation of the province of Transalpine Gaul (later Narbonensis), foundation of Aquae Sextiae (122) and Narbo (118)
wars.summary: Called in by Massalia against the Saluvii, Rome campaigned beyond the Alps for the first time and, after defeating the Allobroges and the Arvernian king Bituitus in 121, annexed southern Gaul.
wars.detail: Fulvius Flaccus (125) and Sextius Calvinus (124-122) destroyed the Saluvian oppidum of Entremont. The Allobroges sheltered the Saluvian king and were attacked by Domitius Ahenobarbus, who won at Vindalium with elephants; Fabius Maximus crushed a huge Arvernian-Allobrogian army at the Isère. The new province secured the land route to Spain (Via Domitia) and brought Rome into contact with the Aedui as 'brothers', a relationship Caesar later exploited.

phases.t: Campaigns against the Saluvii; Entremont destroyed
War with the Allobroges and Arverni
Organisation; Via Domitia; Narbo founded

wars.name: Jugurthine War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Jugurtha captured; western Numidia given to Bocchus, the rest to Gauda
wars.summary: War against the Numidian king Jugurtha, who had seized the whole kingdom and massacred Italian traders at Cirta; marked by Roman defeats, bribery scandals, Metellus' recovery and Marius' victory, ended by Sulla's diplomacy.
wars.detail: Sallust's monograph turns the war into an indictment of the nobility's greed. Its political consequences outweighed its military ones: the Mamilian commission, Marius' election against the senate's wishes, the enrolment of the capite censi, and the beginning of the Marius-Sulla rivalry over who had captured Jugurtha. Modern historians emphasise the role of Italian and equestrian business interests in pushing for war.

phases.t: Cirta massacre, Bestia's peace, Jugurtha in Rome, Albinus' capitulation
Metellus restores discipline: Muthul, Zama, Thala
Marius: Capsa, the Mulucha, battles near Cirta, Sulla's capture of Jugurtha

scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

wars.name: Cimbrian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; the Cimbri, Teutones and Ambrones annihilated at Aquae Sextiae (102) and Vercellae (101)
wars.summary: Migrating peoples from the north, the Cimbri and Teutones with Celtic allies, destroyed a series of Roman armies culminating at Arausio in 105, before Marius, re-elected consul year after year, destroyed them.
wars.detail: The ancients placed the Cimbri's homeland in Jutland (the 'Cimbric peninsula'); the Teutones' origin is less clear, and Celtic names among their leaders (Boiorix) suggest mixed groups. Defeats at Noreia (113), in Gaul (Silanus 109, Cassius 107) and Arausio (105) created panic at Rome and a lasting 'terror Cimbricus'. Politically the war produced Marius' five consecutive consulships, the gladiatorial drill of Rutilius and the Marian army reforms. It remained the reference point for Caesar's presentation of the Germans fifty years later.

phases.t: Noreia; migrations through Gaul; defeat of Silanus
Defeat of Cassius by the Tigurini; Tolosa; Arausio
Cimbri in Spain; Marius trains his army in Gaul
Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae

wars.name: Second Sicilian Slave War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Athenion killed by Manius Aquillius
wars.summary: A revolt of slaves in Sicily, triggered by the halting of manumissions ordered by the senate for unlawfully enslaved allies, created two rebel kingdoms under Salvius (Tryphon) and Athenion.
wars.detail: Diodorus (from Posidonius) is the main source. The war shows the interplay of Roman imperial manpower needs (the Cimbric levies), the publicani's slave-hunting in Asia, and the harsh plantation system of Sicily.

phases.t: Outbreak; Tryphon king at Triocala; Lucullus at Scirthaea
Servilius fails; Aquillius ends the revolt

scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

wars.name: Social War (Marsic War)
wars.outcome: Military victory for Rome, political victory for the allies: citizenship extended to all Italy south of the Po by the lex Julia (90) and lex Plautia Papiria (89)
wars.summary: The Italian allies (socii) of central and southern Italy, after the murder of Drusus, rose against Rome, formed a state called Italia with its capital at Corfinium, and fought a brutal war that Rome won only by conceding the citizenship they had demanded.
wars.detail: Velleius puts the dead at 300,000. The rebels were the Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes, Frentani, Hirpini, Samnites, Lucanians and others; the Latins, Etruscans and Umbrians largely stayed loyal, encouraged by the lex Julia. Both sides fielded legions trained in the same way and led by men who had served together. The war made the reputations of Sulla, Pompeius Strabo, Marius (briefly) and Metellus Pius, and gave Pompey and Cicero their first service. The Samnites fought on into the civil war of 83-82. The integration of Italy into the citizen body transformed Roman politics, though it took until the 70s for the new citizens to be properly registered.

phases.t: Revolt at Asculum; Italian successes; lex Julia
Roman recovery: Asculum, Sulla in Campania and Samnium; lex Plautia Papiria, lex Pompeia
Mopping up; Samnite and Lucanian resistance merges into the civil war

scholarship: Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)
Brunt, The Fall of the Roman Republic (1988)

wars.name: First Mithridatic War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Peace of Dardanus: Mithridates gives up his conquests, pays an indemnity and surrenders a fleet
wars.summary: Provoked by Roman envoys, Mithridates VI overran Bithynia, Asia and Greece, massacred the Italians in Asia, and was driven back by Sulla's victories at Athens, Chaeronea and Orchomenus, while a rival Marian army under Fimbria fought him in Asia.
wars.detail: The war revealed the depth of Greek hatred of Roman rule and of the publicani. Sulla fought it while declared a public enemy at home, which explains his lenient peace. The Asian cities paid for it with a 20,000-talent fine.

phases.t: Mithridates overruns Asia; the Asiatic Vespers
Sulla in Greece: Athens, Chaeronea
Orchomenus; Fimbria in Asia; Dardanus

scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI (1986)

wars.name: Sulla's first civil war (Bellum Octavianum)
wars.outcome: Sulla took Rome in 88; in 87 Cinna and Marius retook it and massacred their enemies
wars.summary: The first Roman civil war fought with legionary armies: Sulla's march on Rome over the Mithridatic command, followed in 87 by the expulsion and return of Cinna and Marius.
wars.detail: Whatever the precedents of political violence since 133, 88 was a qualitative break: a consul led citizen soldiers into Rome against his political opponents. The Marian-Cinnan reprisals of 87 created the blood feud that Sulla's proscriptions avenged.

phases.t: Sulpician laws; Sulla's march; flight of Marius
Cinna expelled; siege of Rome; Marian massacres

wars.name: Sulla's second civil war
wars.outcome: Sullan victory; proscriptions; Sulla dictator
wars.summary: Returning from the East, Sulla defeated the Cinnan regime's larger but poorly led armies in Italy, culminating in the Colline Gate, while Pompey destroyed its remnants in Sicily and Africa.
wars.detail: The war was also the last act of the Social War: Samnites and Lucanians fought for the Marians, and Sulla's vengeance on Samnium was savage. It ended with the proscriptions and the Sullan settlement, and left Sertorius in Spain.

phases.t: Landing at Brundisium; Tifata; defection at Teanum; burning of the Capitol
Sacriportus, Faventia, Clusium, Colline Gate, Praeneste
Pompey in Sicily and Africa; proscriptions

wars.name: Second Mithridatic War
wars.outcome: Pontic victory at the Halys; status quo restored on Sulla's order
wars.summary: An unauthorised raid on Pontus by Sulla's legate Murena, ended by his defeat at the Halys and Sulla's intervention.
wars.detail: Murena used Mithridates' rearmament as pretext. The episode shows the difficulty of controlling governors at a distance, which Sulla's laws on provincial commands tried to address.

phases.t: Murena raids Pontus
Defeat at the Halys; Gabinius brings Sulla's order

wars.name: Revolt of Lepidus
wars.outcome: Senatorial victory; Lepidus dies in Sardinia; his remnant joins Sertorius
wars.summary: The consul Lepidus attempted to overturn Sulla's settlement by force and was defeated by Catulus and Pompey.
wars.detail: Sallust's Histories begin with this episode and preserve speeches of Lepidus and Philippus. The revolt confirmed Pompey's indispensability and his habit of acquiring commands while a private citizen.

phases.t: Lepidus' programme; rising at Faesulae
Senatus consultum ultimum; defeat at Rome and Mutina

wars.name: Sertorian War
wars.outcome: Roman (Sullan) victory after Sertorius' assassination; Spain pacified by Pompey and Metellus
wars.summary: The Marian exile Sertorius, backed by Lusitanians and Celtiberians, held most of Spain for eight years against Metellus Pius and Pompey, and allied with Mithridates, until he was murdered by his own officers.
wars.detail: The war was a Roman civil war fought largely with Iberian troops. Sertorius' guerrilla skill humiliated Pompey (Lauro) and wore down Metellus; attrition, the loss of his lieutenants, and Roman reinforcements eventually told. Pompey's settlement made him the patron of much of Spain.

phases.t: Sertorius establishes himself; Metellus arrives
Pompey's arrival; Lauro, Italica, Sucro, Saguntum
Attrition; murder of Sertorius; Perperna defeated

wars.name: Third Mithridatic War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Pontus annexed, Armenia reduced to a client, Syria annexed; Mithridates dies 63
wars.summary: After the bequest of Bithynia, Mithridates invaded Roman territory. Lucullus destroyed his army at Cyzicus, conquered Pontus and defeated Tigranes at Tigranocerta, but his army mutinied. Pompey, given the command by the lex Manilia, finished Mithridates, received Tigranes' submission, campaigned in the Caucasus and reorganised the whole East.
wars.detail: The war turned Roman hegemony in the East into direct rule over Anatolia and Syria and brought Rome face to face with Parthia. It also produced the great extraordinary command of the lex Manilia and the wealth that Pompey brought home, whose political use triggered the alliance of 60.

phases.t: Bithynian bequest; Chalcedon; Cyzicus; Cabira
Lucullus in Pontus and Armenia: Tigranocerta, Arsanias, Nisibis
Mutiny; Zela
Pompey: the Lycus, Tigranes' submission, Caucasus, Syria, Jerusalem; death of Mithridates

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

wars.name: Third Servile War (Spartacus' revolt)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Spartacus killed; 6,000 captives crucified
wars.summary: A breakout of gladiators from Capua became a slave army of tens of thousands that defeated praetors and consuls across Italy before Crassus destroyed it.
wars.detail: Unlike the Sicilian revolts, it was fought in Italy itself, while Rome's best armies were with Pompey in Spain and Lucullus in the East. Appian and Plutarch disagree on the slaves' aims; there is no sign of an abolitionist programme. The war gave Crassus and Pompey the leverage for their joint consulship of 70.

phases.t: Breakout; Vesuvius; defeat of praetorian armies
Crixus killed; Spartacus beats the consuls; march north and back
Crassus' command; Bruttian wall; the Silarus

scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

wars.name: Wars against the pirates
wars.outcome: Roman victory; piracy suppressed by Pompey in 67; Cilicia and Crete organised as provinces
wars.summary: Piracy based in Rough Cilicia and Crete, fed by the slave trade and by Mithridates, was fought by Marcus Antonius (102), Servilius Isauricus (78-74), Antonius Creticus (74-71) and Metellus in Crete before Pompey's lex Gabinia command cleared the sea in three months.
wars.detail: The pirates seized grain ships, kidnapped Roman magistrates and young Caesar, and raided Ostia in 68. Pompey's success owed much to his resources and to a policy of resettling surrendered pirates as farmers rather than crucifying them.

phases.t: Marcus Antonius in Cilicia; the law on the pirates
Servilius Isauricus in Cilicia and Isauria; Antonius Creticus' failure
Metellus in Crete; lex Gabinia; Pompey's campaign

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

scholarship: de Souza, Piracy in the Graeco-Roman World (1999)

wars.name: Catilinarian conspiracy and war
wars.outcome: Conspiracy exposed; five leaders executed; Catiline killed at Pistoria
wars.summary: Catiline's conspiracy of indebted aristocrats and ruined Sullan veterans, with a rising in Etruria under Manlius, was exposed and suppressed by the consul Cicero.
wars.detail: Sallust and Cicero, both partisans, are the sources. The execution of citizens without trial under the senatus consultum ultimum became the dominant legal-political issue of the 50s, leading to Cicero's exile.

phases.t: Electoral defeat; Manlius' rising; senatus consultum ultimum; Catilinarian orations; executions
Pistoria

wars.name: Gallic Wars
wars.outcome: Roman conquest of Gallia Comata from the Pyrenees to the Rhine; expeditions to Britain and across the Rhine
wars.summary: In eight campaigning seasons Caesar, as proconsul, defeated the Helvetii and Ariovistus, the Belgae, the Armoricans, raided Britain and Germany, crushed a series of revolts and finally the great rising of Vercingetorix at Alesia, conquering all of Gaul.
wars.detail: Caesar's Commentaries are almost our only source, written for political effect at Rome. Plutarch, drawing on figures in circulation, claims Caesar fought three million men, killed a million and enslaved a million; modern estimates are lower but the human cost was immense. The conquest brought Caesar wealth, a devoted veteran army and the political leverage that led to civil war. Archaeology (Alesia, Gergovia, Uxellodunum, Kessel) increasingly tests his narrative.

phases.t: Helvetii and Ariovistus
Belgae
Veneti and Aquitania
Usipetes and Tencteri; Rhine bridge; Britain
Britain; Atuatuca; siege of Cicero's camp
Punitive campaigns; second Rhine crossing
Vercingetorix: Avaricum, Gergovia, Alesia
Mopping up: Uxellodunum

scholarship: Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)
Holmes, Caesar's Conquest of Gaul (2nd ed. 1911)

wars.name: Crassus' Parthian war
wars.outcome: Parthian victory; Crassus killed at Carrhae; Parthian counter-invasion of Syria repulsed by Cassius
wars.summary: Crassus' unprovoked invasion of Parthia ended in catastrophe at Carrhae; the Parthians followed up with raids into Syria in 52-51.
wars.detail: The war had no senatorial mandate beyond Crassus' provincial command; the tribune Ateius Capito cursed Crassus as he left Rome in November 55. Carrhae fixed the Euphrates frontier and a Roman obsession with avenging the lost eagles that shaped policy from Caesar's planned war of 44 to Augustus' diplomatic recovery in 20.

phases.t: Crassus crosses the Euphrates and garrisons Mesopotamian towns
Carrhae
Parthian raids into Syria; Cassius at Antigonea

wars.name: Caesar's civil war
wars.outcome: Caesarian victory; Caesar dictator; the senatorial oligarchy broken
wars.summary: War between Caesar and the senatorial government led by Pompey, fought in Italy, Spain, Illyricum, Africa, Greece, Egypt and Asia; decided at Pharsalus (48), with further campaigns against the Pompeians at Thapsus (46) and Munda (45).
wars.detail: Caesar presented himself as defending his dignitas and the rights of the tribunes; his opponents as defending the authority of the senate and the laws. His policy of clementia won over Italy and many opponents; his speed repeatedly caught enemies unprepared. The Pompeians' strategy of abandoning Italy and their division of command were fatal. Caesar's own De Bello Civili (to 48) and the anonymous Alexandrian, African and Spanish War narratives are the main sources, the latter of very uneven quality.

phases.t: Italy, Massilia, Ilerda; Curio's defeat in Africa
Dyrrhachium, Pharsalus; death of Pompey
Alexandria and Zela (see Alexandrian War); mutiny in Italy
Africa: Ruspina, Thapsus; Cato's death
Spain: Munda

scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

wars.name: Alexandrian War and the war with Pharnaces
wars.outcome: Caesarian victory; Cleopatra installed as queen; Pharnaces defeated at Zela
wars.summary: Caesar's entanglement in the Ptolemaic succession left him besieged in Alexandria for months; meanwhile Pharnaces II reconquered Pontus, until Caesar defeated him at Zela.
wars.detail: The pseudo-Caesarian Bellum Alexandrinum, probably by Hirtius, covers Egypt, Pontus, Illyricum and Spain in 48-47. The delay gave the Pompeians time to regroup in Africa.

phases.t: Siege in the palace quarter; fire in the harbour; Pharos
Pharnaces beats Domitius Calvinus at Nicopolis
Battle of the Nile; Zela

wars.name: War of Mutina
wars.outcome: Antony defeated and driven over the Alps, but both consuls killed; the victors fell out and Antony returned allied with Lepidus
wars.summary: After Caesar's murder, the senate, led by Cicero, backed Decimus Brutus and the young Octavian against Antony, who besieged Brutus in Mutina.
wars.detail: Cicero's Philippics and letters provide an exceptionally detailed contemporary record, including an eyewitness battle report (Fam. 10.30). The death of both consuls left Octavian's army as the decisive force and led to the triumvirate.

phases.t: Antony takes Cisalpine Gaul; legions defect to Octavian; siege of Mutina
Forum Gallorum and Mutina; Antony joins Lepidus

wars.name: War of the Liberators
wars.outcome: Triumviral victory at Philippi; Brutus and Cassius dead
wars.summary: The triumvirs, after proscribing their enemies at home, defeated Brutus and Cassius, who had raised the resources of the East, in two battles at Philippi.
wars.detail: The largest Roman armies ever to face each other, about 19 legions a side. Philippi ended the republican cause in arms. The settlement after the battle, with Antony in the East and Octavian confiscating land in Italy, set the stage for the next decade.

phases.t: Bononia; lex Titia; proscriptions; liberators seize Syria and Macedonia
Xanthus, Rhodes; Philippi

wars.name: Perusine War
wars.outcome: Octavian's victory; Perusia burned; Octavian master of Italy
wars.summary: Lucius Antonius and Fulvia, exploiting Italian anger at land confiscations for veterans, fought Octavian and were besieged and starved in Perusia.
wars.detail: Antony's own role was ambiguous; his generals in Gaul did not intervene. Hostile sources later accused Octavian of human sacrifice at Perusia. The war consolidated Octavian's hold on the western legions.

phases.t: Confiscations; Lucius Antonius' campaign
Siege of Perusia

wars.name: War against Sextus Pompey
wars.outcome: Triumviral victory at Naulochus; Sextus flees and is executed in 35
wars.summary: Sextus Pompey, holding Sicily and dominating the sea, blockaded Italy's grain until Agrippa built a new fleet and destroyed his at Mylae and Naulochus.
wars.detail: Augustan propaganda called it a war against pirates and runaway slaves. Its end brought the elimination of Lepidus and left Octavian sole master of the West.

phases.t: Sextus takes Sicily; blockade of Italy
Treaty of Misenum
War renewed; Cumae and the storm of Scyllaeum
Agrippa's fleet; Mylae, Naulochus; Lepidus deposed

wars.name: Antony's Parthian war
wars.outcome: Parthians expelled from Roman territory (39-38); Antony's invasion of Media fails (36); Armenia occupied (34)
wars.summary: After the Parthian invasion of 40, Antony's legate Ventidius expelled the Parthians and killed Pacorus; Herod and Sosius took Jerusalem; Antony's own great invasion of Media Atropatene in 36 failed with heavy losses, though he annexed Armenia in 34.
wars.detail: Plutarch's account derives from Antony's officer Quintus Dellius, an eyewitness. The failure of 36 and Antony's dependence on Egypt were central to Octavian's propaganda before Actium.

phases.t: Parthian invasion of Syria, Asia Minor and Judaea
Ventidius' victories: Cilician Gates, Amanus, Gindarus
Jerusalem taken; Herod installed
Antony's invasion of Media; Phraaspa; retreat
Conquest of Armenia; Donations of Alexandria

wars.name: Octavian's Illyrian war
wars.outcome: Roman victory; the Iapydes, Pannonians of Siscia and Dalmatae subdued
wars.summary: Campaigns by Octavian and Agrippa against the Alpine and Illyrian peoples behind Italy's north-eastern frontier, including the sieges of Metulum and Siscia.
wars.detail: Appian's Illyrica, drawing on Augustus' own memoirs, is the main source. The war kept the legions busy and gave Octavian a military record to set against Antony's eastern campaigns.

phases.t: Iapydes; Metulum; Siscia
Dalmatae; Promona; recovery of Gabinius' standards

wars.name: War of Actium (final war of the Republic)
wars.outcome: Victory of Octavian; Antony and Cleopatra commit suicide; Egypt annexed
wars.summary: War declared on Cleopatra in 32; Antony and Cleopatra were blockaded at Actium by Agrippa and defeated at sea on 2 September 31; Octavian took Alexandria in August 30.
wars.detail: Officially a foreign war against Egypt, in reality the last civil war of the Republic. Octavian's victory gave him sole control of the empire and the wealth of Egypt to pay off his armies. Augustan poets turned Actium into a cosmic clash of Roman and Egyptian gods; the fighting itself was brief.

phases.t: Rupture; Antony's will; oath of Italy; declaration of war
Agrippa's blockade; Actium
Invasion of Egypt; deaths of Antony and Cleopatra; annexation
